items.title: Making Reddit Work with Liquid Glass on iOS
items.summary: By Corey Roberts, Senior Software Engineer, Design System (iOS) When Apple introduced Liquid Glass at WWDC, our reactions mirrored the rest of the iOS community’s: this looks amazing, and we have so many questions. Many of us have been iOS engineers long enough to remember the first major shift in Apple's design language: the move from texture-rich skeuomorphism of iOS 6 to the flat, motion-driven aesthetic of iOS 7. Assumptions about layout, controls, navigation, and typography went out the window. Layout code sprouted version checks, and making something feel cohesive across both paradigms was an awkward challenge with no grace period. Liquid Glass reminded me of this experience. We knew this wasn’t going to be a simple “rebuild in Xcode and it works” trick. It changed parts of the app we’d spent years building around: the top and bottom navigation, the safe areas, and the window that houses every screen. Navigation became translucent instead of opaque, heights shifted (particularly on iPhone Air), and insets we’d tuned specifically for opaque bars no longer worked. These weren’t cosmetic issues: they were behavioral. A screen that behaved correctly on iOS 18 no longer looked the part under Liquid Glass. We also couldn’t just move everyone to the new design paradigm. Reddit supports a wide range of iOS versions, and those users had to keep the exact same experience they knew. That’s why we leaned on Reddit’s design system, RPL, so the same components could render in both the pre-Liquid Glass and Liquid Glass paradigms. The iOS app rendered in both pre-Liquid Glass and Liquid Glass design paradigms. The Initial Friction with Liquid Glass The challenge with Liquid Glass was compatibility: we had to support two very different design paradigms at once. Simply updating to the new design and calling it a day would have broken the experience for everyone still using an older version of iOS. We needed to make a set of components look and behave correctly in both places while streamlining our APIs so we wouldn’t cause confusion, code duplication, or unintended behaviors. The problem that was most obvious, and one worth understanding before anything else: opaque content underneath the navigation bar defeats Liquid Glass entirely. Prior to Liquid Glass, our navigation constructs were opaque, and we built our screens to be pinned to the safe area edges to avoid unnecessary rendering under the top and bottom navigation bars. Because our bars were opaque, it didn’t matter if nothing was rendered underneath: you couldn’t see it. Liquid Glass inverts that assumption. The top navigation had a diffusive blur that displayed incoming content contextually, and the bottom navigation became modular and translucent. With our current infrastructure, the effect was lost on us entirely. Instead of a translucent, diffusive bar, we got a flat, cut-off band: a jarring visual bug.  That one symptom is the whole problem in miniature: nothing was wrong with our old code. Rather, the rules underneath it changed, and the assumptions we made under the old rules now produced the wrong result. Multiply that across every screen, and you have this project! Two images showcasing the screen getting clipped near the top and bottom navigation areas, causing an obvious visual discrepancy with Liquid Glass. Uncovering Bugs We started our analysis in iOS 26 Beta 2 by building an alpha version of Reddit and looking through all of our screens for issues. We ended up creating categories for the kinds of visual defects we kept seeing:  Hardcoded navigation heights. Much of our layout code relied on static calculations based on OS and device in use. This was never a robust solution, and Liquid Glass (plus newer hardware, like the iPhone Air) made it obviously wrong. These screens were updated to use the top safe area insets. Warped or misplaced icons. A handful of icons became stretched in Liquid Glass due to assumptions that were made with the size of a button. These were predominantly PNG images, many of which were not moved over to using our vector icon set. If an icon looked squished or oddly sized, it was almost always a bitmap that should have been a vector. In a similar vein, our bottom navigation tab for creating a post became misaligned due to using a custom tab item. Static Colors in Glass. Liquid Glass views have a unique property where they adapt the colors of their content view based on the current trait environment. This conflicted with some of our navigation components, which use color tokens tied to the active Reddit theme, not the surrounding environment the color sits in. Custom title views. Apple changed how content renders in the titleView of the navigation controller. In some instances, custom views could cause the diffusive blur that the navigation bar provides to extend across the entire screen!
